utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for the day. Starting with the Prosecution into.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone. Mark Harmon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone taking part in this trial. Mr. Perisic will be represented by Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, and by your leave, we have two new members Annie Tai and Dana Glassel and of course, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith as co-counsel, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good afternoon, sir, and welcome back. The break has been too long, I ask that you make the declaration once again before you proceed with your testimony. Will the usher please help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated. Mr. Harmon, please get the witness's name on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. One again welcome back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, could you statement your name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miodrag Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are going to be going in and out of the private session because of the nature of the documents I'll being to be showing Mr. Starcevic. If we could now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could, first of all, have on the monitor Prosecution Exhibit 1895.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this is a document that you've seen before. In fact, we've spent some time with it in your previous evidence. You recall that we went through, and you assisted us with identifying and defining what various elements of this document meant. For example, on page -- the page that's in front of you, you defined the term "appointed" as per peacetime establishment. Then you took us through and defined a number of other elements assigned and appointed per peacetime establishment, transferred, and temporarily assigned. When I was looking back through this document, I found a portion that we had not addressed, and so if we could turn to page 11 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S, I'm going to ask you, Mr. Starcevic, to assist us one more time with this document. Mr. Starcevic, you will see in about the middle of the page with the letter B, you'll see the phrase: "Transferred and appointed as per peacetime establishment." Could you assist us in interpreting what that phrase means in respect of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be transferred implies that the person to whom this order applies will go from one garrison to another. In other words, from one garrison, and this is probably stated in the statement of reason, this person is transferred to another garrison; but at the same time by virtue of this order, this person is being appointed to a new post in the new garrison that he is being transferred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So could we focus on number 16 who is the first named person under this transfer and appointment item. It's Cedomir Bulat. Could you just walk us through what happened to Mr. Bulat and what he was ordered to do in this respect: What his previous assignment was, where he was transferred, and where his appointment was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bulat is apparently transferred from the Sarajevo garrison to the Belgrade garrison as the commander of the 40th Personnel Centre -- no, as the commander of the 21st corps of the 40th Personnel Centre. He discharged the usual tasks that such a commander would be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can go back to public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a bit at a loss. I heard transferred from Sarajevo, I don't see Sarajevo written anywhere. I do see 40th Personnel Centre which I would have imagined was in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you go to the bottom of the page, last two words visible in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Previous post, thank you, sorry. Thank you, sir, that helps. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you testified last, Mr. Starcevic, we had a very interesting discussion, and you made a distinction between different types of orders. One order, "naredba," which you define as in a quote, I'm referring to page 5462 of the transcript lines 14 to 16, you defined it as a general regulation or a specific regulation that defines the responsibilities of and duties and rights of individuals." And then you defined "naredjenje," at page 5462, lines 23 to 25, as: "... means issuing an operational command. So a 'naredjenje' command is a provision or a document that is part of the chain of command." Now, what I would like to do, Mr. Starcevic, is look at a series of documents starting with Prosecution Exhibit 1777. If that could be on the monitor, please. I'd like to go to page 81 of the B/C/S and the English is found at 0611-7672. Mr. Starcevic, while these documents are coming up on the screen I know you've seen some but not all of these document, it's been awhile since you were here, so please take your time and review the documents and when you've had an opportunity to do so, I will did you some questions about them. So let me first of all, give you the opportunity to review this document once again, and then I'll ask you some questions about it. Have you had a chance to review it, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I have seen it before, but I've seen it just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. This is a document that is dated the 16th of September, 1995. It emanates from Military Post 9000 in Knin. The author of this document is the Commander Lieutenant-General Mile Mrksic. Now, just for purposes of the record, Knin is located in which country?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, it is in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do on this document, because we have an interesting illustration, in the first line below the order number and the location Banja Luka, the word and the term "naredba" is used and then you see that Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then underneath that term is the other term that we discussed earlier, "naredjenje." So can you just comment on this document. There's two terms, two separate terms that are used. The first is in that first line that says, "With the objective of the carrying out the order of the Chief of General Staff of the VJ, I hereby," and then order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is not a very precise question by asking the witness to comment on a document which leads the witness to guess. The witness provided his definitions of "naredba" and "naredjenje," whereas now the Prosecution is asking him to comment this very document. I don't know what else he can provide other than guess-work. If his definitions are there, then Mr. Harmon should be more accurate in asking questions. If he is asking the witness to tell them what was underlying and what was the thinking of the persons issuing these orders is inappropriate, and I think that this is the line of question that Mr. Harmon is pursuing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know he's going to guess, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply he has been asked to give us a comment and to explain why we have these two terms, "naredba" and "naredjenje." The witness is asked to give an expert comment based on his expertise and experience. That means that he should, by that, be asked to analyse the document where we know that the witness hasn't been in the army since 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you use the word expert now in your response to me? Expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can we please in one word say exactly what the basis of your objection is. You can't now say he is going to guess and then you say we are asking for expert opinion. What is the basis of your objection, and I want one word?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way in which the question is posed requires speculation because the request is for comment regarding the form and not the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that the comment is going to be on form and not content. I think this objection must be overruled. Can you proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, you've discussed the differences between these two types of orders. You have an order in front of you, Prosecution Exhibit 177. It uses the two different terms. Can you comment on the use of the two different terms in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, sorry, I think now your question is different. I thought you wanted him to comments on the word that you now mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not on the use of the two different words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on the use of the word "naredba" in the first paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what possible comment one can make on this. Judging by the language of the document, it turns out that the "naredba" that this letter refers to is a basis for issuing this "naredjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So in this first paragraph, Mr. Starcevic, was there an order issued by the Chief of the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, yes, there's a reference made to his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And based on that order of the Chief of General Staff, what type of an order did Mile Mrksic issue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Mrksic signed is an operational command "naredjenje," that is to carry out a task that has been specified in the chief's order or "naredba."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm done with this document, Your Honour. If I could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1925, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's, first of all, look at this document. Let me be clear, Mr. Starcevic, do you recall having seen this document before coming into court today? And if not, if you need time to review it, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember having seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's go through this document then, we'll go through it slowly. If we could start at the top, we could see, first of all, this document is dated the 24th of March, 1995. And it emanates from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia cabinet of the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. And if we could turn to the last page in each of these documents, we will see who is the author of this document. Do you see who the author of this document is, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, Lieutenant-General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we return to the first page of each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, we can see in this document that in the caption below the date it says: "Order for the formation of a coordinating staff for assistance to the 40th Personnel Centre." And we can see in the Serbian language version of that, it uses the term "naredjenje." Now, if we go to the bottom of the English there is the word order. If we look at the corresponding word in the Serbian version it says "naredjenje." And is this document, Mr. Starcevic, a command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this is a "naredjenje," a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the command that was issued, we can see in Roman numeral I is to form a coordinating staff comprised of specific individuals. You see that in the text?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we take, for example, number 2, there's a -- we'll stay with this page then. If we go to number 2 we can see one of the individuals is a retired major-general from the association of veterans. If we go to number 3, we can see this person is from the VJ General Staff logistics sector. If we could focus on 7 and 8, we can see that both of those individuals are -- number 7 is a member of the VJ General Staff personnel administration 40th Personnel Centre department of personnel affairs; and number 8 is communications colonel of the Main Staff of the 40th Personnel Centre. Now, in respect of this command, is this a proper exercise by General Perisic of command over members who are in the 40th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally looking at it, you could conclude that. However, what is confusing is the fact that there is a person here who is not actually a member of the army. He is retired. So it's hard for anybody to be able to command him. Also the fact that is creating a little more confusion is that this is evidently being formed not as a permanent organisational unit but as some sort of temporary force or composition which can be seen from the fact that none of those that have General Perisic as their superior is changing their own regular establishment duties, but are doing their work in the coordination HQ on top of their regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So insofar as items number 7 and 8, members of the 40th Personnel Centre, would that be a proper exercise of command over those individuals? Putting aside for just the moment item number 2 who is Mr. Bajic -- retired General Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that you could make that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I take it your reservation only relates to a retired general and whether the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army could issue a command to a retired person? Is that your reservation, if I understood it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small intervention on the transcript page 10, line 17. The witness said Perisic [In English] Not changing their regular establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just about to raise that with you too, Mr. Harmon. That as I understand the witness, that's not the only reservation, the reservation also is that, one, how does this become an order if it is ordered to a person who is retired who cannot be ordered. Number one. Number two, number two, how does it become an order to members of the -- active members of the army when they are not being relieved of their previous responsibilities. They are being required to carry on this while they are also still required to maintain their previous responsibilities. Number three, that this order appears to be of a -- the commission rather, appears to be of a temporary nature and not a permanent order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I can address those, and I'll ask questions of the witness. I think in respect, first of all, Your Honours, in respect of the order, the command given to a retired person, I think Mr. Starcevic has made that clear. He says that's dubious nature of whether it can be given or can't be given is something that he has reservation on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask some additional questions to you, Mr. Starcevic. When a commanding officer -- strike that. When an officer is in a particular position performing specific tasks, can a superior officer, in addition to those specific tasks the officer is performing, command him to do something else, some additional tasks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough in my first answer. The fact that their basic duties are not being changed, the duties that that they were appointed to, but that they are being entrusted with tasks in the coordination staff can, in fact, lead to the conclusion that the coordination staff is not a newly formed unit, but a kind of temporary body that is being formed because of some particular needs, to assist, as one can see in the preamble, to help the 40th Personnel Centre. Still, they remain on their own -- on their primary duties and provide help when that is essential, provide help to this coordination staff on top of their regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Does that resolve the Court's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was resolved a long time ago. All I was saying the one you mentioned was not the only basis on which the witness was saying -- basing his argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 9471 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I know you have not had an opportunity to see this document before we came into court, so I will, first of all, orient you through this a bit and then I will give you an opportunity to take a look at this document. On the first page we can see that this document emanates from Slobodan Peric, who is a colonel. He is commander of the 18th SVK Corps. The date of the document is 20 June, 1995, and the document is being submitted to the chief of the VJ General Staff. If we turn to the last page of the document, we can see who signed this. And you see a name at the end of this document, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Slobodan Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn back to the first page then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Starcevic, I want to go to the first paragraph that is above small letter (a). It says: "Based on your oral order, I am submitting to you the list of officers who participated and those who did not participate in combat operations of the 18th Corps from 1 to 2 May, 1995, in the territory of Western Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you take a look at the term "order" in this example, it is using the word "naredjenje" you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this, the type of an order that Colonel Peric received was a command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, judging by what it says in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, if this item could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2412.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if it could be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return to public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 1827 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this is a document -- I'll give you some time to look at it. I believe you may have seen this before you came into testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes, but I cannot be sure. A lot of time has passed since then, but I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree, a lot of time has passed, so I want to give you the opportunity to look at this. This is a document, sir, that is dated the 11th of April, 1994. It comes from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and it is directed to the Main Staff of the Army of Srpska. Can we go to the bottom to see who is the author of this document. Can you tell us who is the author of this document, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, if we can go back --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a warning, from what we can see in the document. Can you assist us in what is the meaning of a warning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have the legal significance of a warning. It's a colloquial act or document which doesn't have a legal form or legal binding effect. It can be understood also as advice or a proposal or a recommendation. And there is no formal legal warning in the form of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I correct your attention to the second item in the warning. It says: "Maintain decisive defence of all axes and regions, focussing on the Posavina corridor." Do you know where the Posavina corridor is, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know where that corridor is in the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you locate that for us, or can you assist us where that is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the section of the road between -- well, between the towns of Banja Luka and Bijeljina. It would be best to say more closely between Brcko and Bijeljina. It's practically the only link between two parts of Republika Srpska, the only road, the only transport link between two parts of Republika Srpska, the western part and the eastern part, and then on to link with the Republic of Serbia. It is located in the northern area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right next to the river Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, have you heard of the six strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you heard of it unofficially?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About some of them, yes, but that is something that falls under being informed in general and monitoring or following the situation and finally out of my own personal views about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And based on the information that you collected, Mr. Starcevic, was the creation and maintenance of the corridor linking Banja Luka and Bijeljina one of the objectives, one of the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serb people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Harmon now is leading the witness. He could have asked him what does he know what the strategic goals are, but now he has, in this manner, suggested the answer. And then I think he continues to suggest the follow-up questions that relate to this document, so as a whole, this way of questioning is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I tried not to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am afraid you did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You failed dismally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- Mr. Starcevic, you need some water?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there water for the witness? Just check and see, please. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment then, Mr. Starcevic, on what relationship, if any, the Posavina corridor had to strategic objectives, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course again I'm placed in the position of voicing my own position on that, but I have no problem in doing that. I believe that it was inevitable to maintain the corridor. It was simply requisite for keeping the connection between two parts of Republika Srpska; otherwise without the corridor, the two parts would have been cut off from one another and have had no link with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with this document, Your Honour. Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we remove it and go into private session. Sir, you said the word "warn" has no legal consequences. What would be the consequences if the warning had not been heeded? Could the issuer of this warning take any measures against those who disobeyed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe that any legal measures could have been taken should someone fail to adhere to the warning, but in view of the fact that a warning is in a way a question of good services or an advice, perhaps there could be some influence on the quality of the relationship between the person who is issuing the warning and -- or the side that is issuing the warning and the side that does not adhere to the warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the document be removed and may the Chamber move into open session. That's what you asked for, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want private session. I beg your pardon. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 766 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the document that is in front of you are minutes from the 45th Session of the Supreme Defence Council that was held on the 5th of October, 1995. It identifies in that document the participants in that. And I'd like to direct your attention and the Court's and the Defence attention to item number 3, which is found on the next page. First of all, familiarise yourself with that again, if you would, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see from item 3 that the text discusses the termination of professional military service of four generals who were members of the 40th Personnel Centre. It identifies them as Mile Mrksic, Novakovic, Celeketic, and Bjelanovic. It says that these people had, in accordance with the Law on the Yugoslav Army, Article 107, paragraph 2, returned to the Yugoslav Army after the fall of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about other elements in this particular paragraph, but if we could very briefly, I want to focus your attention on what the meaning of Article 107, paragraph 2, means in this paragraph. First of all, I would like to go back to Article 107, and you can assist us. Can I quickly go to Prosecution Exhibit197, and we can focus on Article 107 in that. I'm particularly interested this page 25 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. Now, Mr. Starcevic, maybe you can help us out on this. The minutes of this SDC session says, and I quote, it identifies the four generals and it says: "Who had in accordance with the law on Yugoslav Army, Article 107, paragraph 2, returned to the Yugoslav Army after the fall of the RSK." Can you direct us to which portion of Article 107 this text refers to? So Article 107 is in front of you, and the text of the SDC, I'll reread it, it says that these four generals had: "In accordance with the Law on the Yugoslav Army, Article 107, paragraph 2, returned to the Yugoslav Army after the fall of the RSK." Which portion of the Article 107 is being referred to in particular SDC minute? The reason I ask you is -- go ahead, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the interpretation is wrong. They didn't return pursuant to Article 107. Simply it is being noted that they had returned to the Army of Yugoslavia. Article 107 is used for the grounds of termination of duty, not those who return pursuant to Article 107, but their service will be terminated pursuant to Article 107, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I thank you very much for that clarification, it wasn't clear to me from the text I had in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go back then to Prosecution Exhibit 766 in item 3 that we were looking at just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's take a look at -- let me take a look at then -- if Article 107, paragraph 2, is the basis for their termination, Article 107, paragraph 2, deals with people who have served 30 years in the service; correct? Let me just get 107 in front of me again. Paragraph -- Article 107, paragraph 2. Paragraph 2 that I have in front of me, Mr. Starcevic, I'd ask you to confirm this: "Military service of a professional officer or a non-commissioned officer shall be terminated when he has acquired at least 30 pensionable years of service if the needs of the service so require." That's the basis then that the SDC terminate these individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether this is a good translation or maybe you have misspoken. It is either when they have 30 years of service, or if it is necessary, and that is to say he will remain in the service after those 30 years if the service needs/requires so. So this is the basis to which item 3 is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when a person is terminated on that basis, Mr. Starcevic, administratively, what are the procedural rights of the person being terminated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His procedural right is to have an interview with officer in charge. In this particular case this is the Chief of Staff, who informed these officers about the decision already taken by the Supreme Defence Council. He probably also explains the reasons to them for such a decision, although that is not a necessity and binding, and this is followed by preparing the papers for service termination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would a person who is being terminated on the basis of Article 107, paragraph 2, be entitled to full rights and benefits up to the actual day when that person leaves the service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They retain all the rights and benefits up to the moment of handing over the duty. The handover of duty is an official procedure which means that this person signs that he has handed over his duty as of that date, and that date is then counted as the date of termination of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we take a look at item 3, I just want to point out some additional features to it. We looked at the date of these minutes which is October 15th, 1995, and we can see in the first paragraph that the Supreme Defence Council decided to pass an enactment which retroactively retired these four generals. In other words, they were to be retired as of the 31st of December, 1994. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Furthermore, in the second paragraph, that the General Perisic was tasked with conducting an interview of those four generals in order to inform them of the decision of the Supreme Defence Council, and to inform them of their duty to place themselves at the disposal of the 30th Personnel Centre following their termination from military service in the Yugoslav Army. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look now at a series of documents, if we could. We can return to public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we have Prosecution Exhibit 1910 on the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at that for just a minute, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see that this document is an Official Note. The author of this Official Note is General Perisic, and the date at the bottom left-hand side is the 6th of October, 1995, one day following the 45th Session of the SDC, and this is an Official Note relating to an interview with Major-General Milan Celeketic. And it indicates that there was an interview, and it indicates that General Celeketic agreed to the termination of military service on the 31st of December, 1994, pursuant to Article 107, paragraph 2, of the Law on the Yugoslav Army, and he accepted to be sent to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next exhibit in order, which is Prosecution Exhibit 1908.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me when you've had a chance to review this, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's -- this is -- this is a decree of the president of the FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it's dated the 22nd of December, 1994. It relates to the termination of professional military service for major -- I mean, Milan Celeketic, who was on duty at the 40th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the bottom of the document to see whose name appears on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see a name who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Zoran Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what is the basis for the termination of General Celeketic, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we have to make a distinction between the base and the reason. The base is Article 107, paragraph 2, and the reason was that because the officer in charge made an assessment and decided that his service should be terminated because that is the requirement of the service, and that was the discretionary right of the person -- of the decision-maker, who in this particular instance is the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document bears the date of December 22nd, 1994. The decision of the SDC, as we saw earlier, was in 1995; correct? The minutes of the 45th Session was the 5th of October, 1995. My question to you, Mr. Starcevic, is there a provision in the FRY law that permits the backdating of presidential decrees?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no such provision. It would be illusionary if something like that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your many years in the military service, have you ever seen decree, an official decree that has been backdated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I'm not sure. It was possible, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am finished with that document. Can we turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1909, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, this is a document dated the 30th of December, 1994, from Military Post 1790. And it is a decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the English and the Serbian version of this document to see who the author of this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of this document is Major-General Dusan Zoric. If I remember correctly, he was the chief of the personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The personnel administration of which army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go back to the page number 1, we can see exactly without assuming. Yes, the Army of Yugoslavia or the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you, in terms of the legal basis for issuing this document, if you look at the first paragraph of the document, it refers to Article 153 of the Law on the Yugoslav Army. You see that reference?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you recall what 153 of the Law on the Army is, or should we together take a look at Article 153 just to complete the record on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have Prosecution Exhibit 197, please, and if we could refer to Article 153.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for one minute. I'm just waiting for the English version to appear on the screen. So in this case, Mr. Starcevic, 153 relates to the discharge being issued by a superior officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. This decision, therefore, what was the relationship, therefore, based on this document of the author of this document, Major-General Dusan Zoric to Major-General Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say off the top of my head, but if my memory serves me well, the document on discharge of the general is, as a rule, issued by the head of the administration. This document is part of the procedure that we discussed the termination of service. So it is preceded by an order, then the person in charge has to hand over the duty, and the discharge document is issued, which is, by its nature, a declaratory document. It is just noted that his service has been terminated based on a decision of the officer in charge, that all the legal terms and requirements have been fulfilled, and that as of that date, he ceases to be a professional serviceman. I'm not sure, but I think that the order on powers and responsibilities assigned at the time by the Chief of Staff and before that the federal minister stipulates that in case of generals, these documents shall be issued by the chief of the personnel department, or administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we please return on the monitor to Prosecution Exhibit 1909, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down on the English version on the left. That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see, Mr. Starcevic, I want to direct your attention to two elements in this document. The first is the date, that this document was issued by General Zoric, it's the 30th of December, 1994. And in the text of the document under "statement of reasons," it said that this order was delivered to General Celeketic on the 25th of December, 1994; and on the 30th of December, 1994 General Celeketic filed a report that on that particular day he had handed over his duties. You have seen the date of the minutes of the 45th Session of the SDC that gave rise to the retroactive retirement of General Celeketic. Can you comments on the dates on those portions of the document I just directed your attention to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know how to comment on it. If we take these dates into consideration in the order on the termination of service and the discharge from service as relevant ones, and the time when the Supreme Defence Council met, Celeketic was no longer in the army; therefore, I don't know if it's possible that these documents were really issued on the dates that they bear, and then were subsequently not executed or implemented, and I don't know for what reasons. Or it may be that the case that they simply put in the dates afterwards, but I really have no grounds for making such comments. This would require a very focused investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, because I asked you earlier, Mr. Starcevic, about the backdating of decrees. Is there anything in the VJ law on the army or any other VJ laws that permit the backdating of decisions issued by the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I asked Mr. Starcevic about the -- anything in the law that dealt with the backdating of decrees. I'm now focussing on a decision of the VJ. My question is slightly different: Is there anything in the VJ law that relates to the backdating of decisions as opposed to decrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you understand what Mr. Harmon has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and in that case, I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know -- don't know of any such provision, and it would be completely illogical for a law to contain such a provision because such documents are related to specific individual rights. Now we are in the area of philosophical and legal questions; therefore, it is impossible to provide such stipulations in the law. The only exception is if you have a declaratory document that describe the already-existing factual situation and unnecessary in order to ensure that a certain legal procedure is implemented. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. For example, if somebody was killed somewhere and then his death is found out only six months later, then in such instances, it is permissible to issue a document saying that his service terminated on the date of his death. But, of course, this does not effect any rights or entitlements of his family up to the time when this fact was found out. So I'm talking now here about a factual situation, not a legal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: A retroactive retirement, in this circumstance, would affect rights and entitlements of General Celeketic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, looking at P1909, what effect, if any, would a retroactive decision to retire General Celeketic have on his rights and his entitlements?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, if it happened retroactively, Celeketic was receiving a salary for the whole period as if he had been working, and he also received all the benefits and fringe benefits as if he were working. That means that he would be entitled to retain all these rights. No one would be able to take away that from him because they retired him retroactively. After all, during the whole procedure and in every stage thereof, had a legal possibility to file for the protection of his rights by lodging a complaint to the Supreme Court and instigating a proceedings if he deemed that these documents were an infringement of his rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 1918, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask one or two questions before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Based on the exception that you referred to, Mr. Starcevic, of a declaratory order, if, indeed, Mr. Celeketic was actually and factually retired in 1994, but the legal document that relate to his retirement were only issued on the 5th of October, 1995, would it not be possible for that situation to fall within that exception that you mentioned just to declare that he is retired as of 1994? Supposing he didn't work since 1994 December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe in some extreme situation, but it is simply incredible. The only possibility would be for him to have stopped working in 1994, that he didn't come to work at all, that he was not doing his duty, that he was away from the garrison; but if that was the case, he would be subject to disciplinary responsibility. Each superior officer of his would then be obliged to stop his pay. Therefore, I think, that in this specific case, it is difficult to qualify this act or this document as a declaratory one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in that case would it be logical or would it be appropriate to say that he received the order on the 25th of December when he received it much later, December 1994, when, in fact, the documentation is being drafted in October 1995? Or would everything be dated as of the time of documentation but would the fact of retroactivity be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if we accept this as a theoretical possibility that you have just described, but nevertheless, it wouldn't be possible, and it musn't be put in the document that the document was handed over to him on the 25th of December, 1994; rather another document should be issued stipulating that there is such a theoretical possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. You may proceed. You asked for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 1918, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's just identify this document for the record. This is a document, it is dated the 24th of May, 2003. It is a request for payment of unpaid salaries, and it's addressed to the Military Post 1790 in Belgrade. If we could go to the -- actually, you can see on the right-hand side a name of an individual. Whose name appears at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go in the English to the previous page. In the previous page, the first paragraph I want to direct your attention to, General Celeketic says: "As a retired active officer of the former JNA and the VJ, due to the needs on the service and acting on your orders, I served in units of the former JNA, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the Army of Serbian Krajina in the Republic of Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1 April 1991, to 31 October 1995, when my professional military service was ended by decree." And then it talks about the FRY Presidency of 22 December, 1994? Now, this in part, does it not, Mr. Starcevic, clarify the actual term of service in the army that General Celeketic served?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this actually creates even more confusion because Celeketic, himself, asserts that he was in service until the 31st of October, 1995, and refers to the decree of the Presidency dated the 22nd of December, 1994. Thus, in the introductory part before making his request, he brings into question what we have discussed so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a further point, Mr. Starcevic. Taking the first paragraph at its face value that General Celeketic served in active service in the JNA, the VRS, and the SVK, up until 31 October, 1995, would he be entitled to his, his pension benefits and other military benefits, up through and including 31st October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle. Yes, but I wasn't precise enough here maybe because I cannot remember right now when the decision on termination of service was adopted because theoretically there was the possibility that his service be terminated pursuant to that decree. But perhaps he would not step down in time because only once the document on termination is adopted does his status of professional soldier end. A certain amount of time can pass from the adoption of the document on the termination of service until he is fully divested, but until that time, he continues to carry out his duties; but, in any event, up to the 31st of October, 1995, he does enjoy all the rights due to him on the basis of the work he is performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've finished with this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just want to come back and clarify one element, Mr. Starcevic, in your testimony in the last session. I just want to be perfectly clear because I want to take you back to Article 107 just briefly. And I want to just clarify one portion of the transcript that I received of your answer. And I'm referring to page 20 of the previous session. It is at lines 23 to 25. Now, we were discussing, Mr. Starcevic, the meaning of Article 107, paragraph 2, and I had read what is my translation, which Mr. Starcevic, which reads that the military -- are you okay, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Which reads: "'The military service of a professional officer or a non-commissioned officer shall be terminated when he has acquired at least 30 pensionable years of service if the needs of the service so require.'" Now, the answer that is recorded that you provided was as follows: "A. I'm not quite sure whether this is a good translation or maybe you have misspoken. It is either when they have 30 years of service," or if it is necessary. Now, let me ask you this question to clarify that: Is it when they have 30 years of service and if it is necessary, or is it 30 years of service or if it is necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that before the witness answers, I think that it would be fair to let the witness see that article and read it out before he gives his answer so that way he doesn't have to interpret it. As far as I can remember, he spoke on the basis of his recollection, so I think the adequate article should be placed in front of him so that he can read it in the courtroom. I think that would be the best explanation or the best option for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. It's Prosecution Exhibit 197, it's Article 107. I thought we had done that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And my point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess Mr. Lukic is just being assisting you to make sure that our witness is precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the word I'm interested in clarifying is whether there is an alternative. If it is either 30 years of service or if it is necessary. So it's the word "or" that I want to focus your attention on. So if we have Article 107 in front of you, if you can look at paragraph 2, having looked at that, can you provide us with an answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember what was in dispute. I heard in translation that you said when he has 30 years of service or a decision on that is made by the authorised senior officer. This is what I intervened about, the actual meaning of the article is, once he fulfills 30 years of service, if a decision is made by the authorised senior officer. In any case, it is necessary to meet both conditions, that he has at least 30 years of service and that the authorised superior officer makes the decision that this is something that is required by the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you very much, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to Prosecution Exhibit 2203.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see in the Serbian language version, I see what this document is. I don't see that in the English version yet, the corresponding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm advised that there is no English translation of the first page; therefore, we don't have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that case, if we could rely on the witness to read just the first page of the Serbian version then I'm going to direct his attention to other elements in this particular section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does it come that this was admitted that form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I don't have an answer for you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know why it was tendered in that form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm torn between two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to remind you that the status of this document is MFI, as far as I know. All of the documents from this group are MFI marked documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would explain why it was admitted in that form then, most probably.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, I've been listening and carrying on multiple conversations, Your Honour. Let me just catch up with the dialogue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The dialogue was that it is an MFI document and the Registrar advises that it was part of a bundle that was tendered by Mr. Randal. I suppose that's why it was MFI'd; therefore, it's still to be checked, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently, we do not have an English translation of this first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But may I just explore with the witness what this says so it's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you identify what this first page says and what the date is of this particular session?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the recording of the collegium of the chiefs of the general -- of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia held on the 6th of November, 1995, which is not authorised or corrected, as far as I can see. Yes, it's not corrected. This is a tape recording of the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to direct everyone's attention, and your attention, Mr. Starcevic, to the English page 4 and 5 of this, starting with page 4. And the B/C/S starting at page 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Harmon, I just want -- now that we don't have a translation of this first page, I just want to understand what this document is all about. It is translated as a collegium of the chiefs of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Is this a collegium of the chief? Or it is a collegium of the chiefs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness what his understanding of it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you assist us in that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the heading, it is a collegium of the chief of staff, Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in the Serbian also the meaning of this word -- actually in this case, the plural and the singular in the Serbian could be indicated, so in English it was translated as the plural. But, actually, I don't think that is the meaning of it, so perhaps the interpreters could pay attention to that. The way it has been entered into the transcript right now, we are talking about the plural chiefs, maybe you can ask the witness again whether he meant the singular or the plural, I think perhaps it's the erroneous interpretation of the word in Serbian which can, in this form, indicate both the singular and the plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Over to you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I refer to page 37. If I go to 37 of the transcript, it's now moving up and down, I just need some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Click on the red button.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 36, I thought the witness had answered this in the singular. He said at line 11, 10 and 11: "This is a recording of the collegium of the chiefs," and then he corrected himself, "of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia." So I thought the record was clear from the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought so, but I heard Mr. Lukic say the word in B/C/S could be either plural or singular. And he was asking that the witness be asked to specifically state whether he really intended to use the singular or the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, perhaps you can assist us then. Did you intend to use the plural form or the singular form?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did look. I think that the problem is line 24 on page 36, and I think that there is some confusion there in the interpretation of the entire sentence. Perhaps I would like to help a little bit with my modest knowledge of English. Line 24 on page 36, unfortunately I'm not able to see it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 24, on my page 36, sir, is Mr. Harmon: "Let me ask the witness, Your Honour." Let me see on the other LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to be totally of use, without complicating, I think that the matter is simple. The way it's entered into the transcript is something that bothers me. The witness can just be asked whether he meant the singular or the plural, and I will not have any problems with it. I think page 37, line 1 again refers to chiefs of staff. Look, in his answer, the interpretation into English on line 1, page 37, also says chiefs of staff, and I really think that the witness did not mean to say that. So perhaps it will be quite easy to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just put the question again to the witness. He doesn't have to look at the transcript. Did he intend the singular or the plural?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But I will ask you again, Mr. Starcevic, did you intend the singular form or the plural form?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the singular because there are no chiefs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. There's only one Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. And on the title page, this is the collegium of that one Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I, in respect of that document, P2203, could I have the English. And the English version I'm interested in is 0618-6912ET, starting with page 44 of the B/C/S. We are having some difficulty getting this document up, Your Honour. It is English version, page 4. If you go down, could you scroll up on the English version, please. The other direction, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like to direct your attention to, Mr. Starcevic, is the bottom paragraph where it says, it's General Perisic speaking, and it says: "Okay, here we have a dilemma ..." And when you get to the end of that, it will carry over to the next page. And I'd like you to read that portion of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go back, I want to make sure the Judges have an opportunity to see. Can we go back please, I need to let the Judges take a look at this as well, and, Mr. Starcevic, I need you to take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, when you are finished looking at the B/C/S version of this, it will carry over to the next page, and if you give me a signal that you need to go to the next page, then I can direct the Registrar to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if we can enlarge it a little bit because I cannot see it well enough to be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've read it a long time, but I just don't understand what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, well we have to go to the next page then, Your Honour. If we could go to the second page of the English, and when Mr. Starcevic gives me the signal, if we could go to the second page of the B/C/S, we can understand the full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So tell me when you finish, Mr. Starcevic, and I will ask you some questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph, the beginning of this comments by General Perisic, he says that if someone is to blame the most beside those four, I'm saying the ones which we have pensioned off, "he," referring to someone else, "is the most guilty one." If we carry on in that paragraph in that discussion or in those comments by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a procedural problem here. We wanted this document to be MFI'd because the Defence disputes the authenticity of this document. The witness has read this document. Now that Mr. Harmon is reading the document, it becomes a part of the transcript, and we still dispute the authenticity of the document. So now we object to the fact that a part of the document that we dispute is being entered into the transcript. Mr. Harmon knows why we are objecting to the authenticity of this document, and he can put certain facts to the witness, but I'm not sure whether it's okay for certain parts of this document to be read into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only way I can ask precise questions about this text is to quote the version I have in front of me. If the document turns out not to be authentic, the Court can disregard the questions I put to the witness and the answers he gives. So I think that Mr. Lukic's concern can be taken care of by the procedure that I've suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, then we'll expunge whatever needs to be expunged, if the need should arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, in this text that we have -- that you have seen, General Perisic says: "And I wrote to the Supreme Defence Council that all four of them should be prosecuted. 'Is it in your interest that they would be prosecuted?'" And then there's brackets "he or they said yes," and "'is it in your interest that that would not be made public?'" Another quotation: "Yes. And now if we pension them off and then prosecute them, there are different sanctions than if we do not pension them off and prosecute them. And they said as it was necessary to calm things down and not to make public, then they made a solemn decision to pension off all four of them, and they pensioned them off." So my first question, Mr. Starcevic, is: These persons were members of the 40th Personnel Centre, which was a formation within the Yugoslav Army. Did General Perisic have the authority to investigate, to discipline, and to refer these persons for Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, just by itself, doesn't allow me to make any conclusions. You cannot quite clearly see here who these people are. They are referred to as "they," so I can conclude who these four persons could be, but I don't see what the connection would be between them and the 40th Personnel Centre. However, General Perisic did not have the authority to prosecute somebody or wave them from being prosecuted. He could initiate disciplinary proceedings against them if he happened to be their superior or spare them from that, but the right to exonerate them, or the right to wave them from criminal prosecution is something that only the president of the republic has as a right, not General Perisic. I don't know whether this text refers to him or not. It doesn't actually provide much room for any kind of precise conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that text seems to be his speech in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this text, Mr. Starcevic, refers to the four of them, assuming, Mr. Starcevic, that the four of them refers to the four generals who were retroactively retired and pensioned off, my question is the same: Did General Perisic have the authority to initiate an investigation, to discipline them and to refer them for prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these are the four general, one of whom was Celeketic, and the others were in the same position as he was and were members of this personnel centre, General Perisic could have initiated a disciplinary procedure against them. However, as for criminal prosecution, his only power was to file a criminal report to the Prosecutor's Office in charge, who would then decide whether there were grounds for prosecution or not. But he definitely did not have an authority to file any form of bill of indictment or charges or to take any decision that would -- that would relieve them or release them of any criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to slightly change the question, Mr. Starcevic. Had these four generals not been members of the 40th Personnel Centre, they had just been generals serving in the SVK, but without being members of the 40th Personnel Centre, would General Perisic have had the ability to discipline them or to sanction them or refer them for prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that with this question Mr. Harmon has gone beyond the limit of your decision on questioning Mr. Starcevic. What Mr. Starcevic can offer as his expert experience. The framework of his questioning should be limited to what he knows personally while he was in a certain position. The questions asked by Mr. Harmon are formally of the same nature as those answered by him about a month ago when he explained the law to us. We, on that occasion, received quite clear answers what the law says about the authorities of the Chief of Staff. Mr. Harmon is now asking Mr. Starcevic to interpret something which is based on facts and which goes beyond what the expertise that he is capable of talking about. He is putting forward to him an assumption based on a fact, and is seeking to elicit from him an expert opinion which transgressed the limits of the framework set up for this witness. Let us assume that these are the four generals, and then based on that assumption, he wants to arrive at the conclusion to which he already provided an answer when he explained a month ago what the authority of the Chief of Staff or any other officer had in terms of disciplinary measure. This is all he can say, and this pertains to the law, what he explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the objection is. Whether the objection is the question that has been asked and answered before, or whether the objection is that the question calls for an expert opinion. If the question is that it calls for an expert opinion, the Court, in its decision, permitted this witness, based on his experience, to give opinions. And this question that I've asked this witness relates to, one, the law on the army; and, two, whether or not General Perisic had the competencies to discipline, refer for discipline, sanctions, or refer for prosecution, persons who were not in the VJ. That was the question. I think that this witness can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought the question was, but you see the difficulty here is that objections some in pages and pages of speeches, and I never know what the basis is. And I've tried to say can we get the basis of an objection in one sentence. That would make it easier for the Chamber to rule. I've heard several arguments. As you say, is it because the question is asked and answered, is it because we've been asking for expert opinion that goes beyond the scope of the expert's expertise. I really don't know. But as I understand, Mr. Lukic, I don't know whether you said that the witness is here to tell us on the law. I guess, if that is what you are saying, then the question becomes competent. Perhaps, it's based on facts, then it's something else. And the legal question is, does the Chief of Staff of the - how do you call it, you don't call it the Main Staff, you call it the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- General Staff of the VJ have the legal authority to punish people who are not members of the VJ; is there a legal provision that provides for that? That's the nub of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that basically this witness discussed this a month ago when he explained the law and the authority of the Chief of Staff of the VJ, and I see this as a repetition. If you want me a precise reference, I would ask for some time to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, that's the objection. Question asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have a precise reference to that, but if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic offers. Mr. Lukic, reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection withdrawn. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, you may provide us with an answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, the question was, and the question was then repeated by the presiding judge, whether General Perisic had an authority to discipline someone who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was in the Spanish Army, a member of the Spanish Army, not a member of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, his authority pertains solely to members of the VJ, Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Starcevic. Now, let me just focus on any procedural differences in the law between somebody being prosecuted for misdeeds or omissions and somebody being retroactively retired for -- for reasons that they had served 30 years in the service and the needs of the service required their termination from service. What procedural differences would be available to persons in those situations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the criminal offence for which a person is prosecuted. Serious crimes require that this person be removed from duty, but the final decision on his status in the service is pending the completion of the criminal proceedings, that is to say, until this person is found guilty or not guilty.
